vulnerabilities.summary: Pillow: EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit
vulnerabilities.details:
``` ============================================================================ EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit Location: src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:92 in Ghostscript() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` When an application opens an untrusted Encapsulated PostScript file and asks Pillow to render it at a larger scale, Pillow has Ghostscript produce an image several times bigger than Pillow's configured size limit allows. The size check runs only after Ghostscript has finished rendering and written the full raw image to a temporary file. An attacker who can upload a file of about 100 bytes makes each such request spend scale² times the Ghostscript rendering work and temporary disk space that the limit is meant to permit. For example, at scale 2 that is a 972 MB temporary file. The cause is in `Ghostscript()` in `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`. It multiplies the file-declared size by the caller's `scale` (lines 93-94) and passes the product to `gs` as the `-g` output geometry. It never calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` on the scaled size. The only check is the one `Image.open()` ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and `load(scale=2)` then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. `DecompressionBombError` fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption. The effect is a constant-factor overshoot rather than an unbounded one, for three reasons: * The multiplier is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file. * With the default warning filter, `Image.open()` already lets files up to 2× the limit reach Ghostscript at `scale=1`. * Any application feeding untrusted files to Ghostscript is already exposed to a tiny file that keeps Ghostscript busy indefinitely, since `gs` runs with no timeout. This is the EPS counterpart of the WMF `load(dpi)` gap closed in af70b075a. It has been present since the decompression-bomb limit was introduced in ce2955ec7 (2.5.0). The attached reproducer stubs out Ghostscript and shows a 76-byte file passing `Image.open()` and reaching `gs` with `-g18000x18000`. A one-line patch mirroring the WMF check is included. ## Details `EpsImageFile.load(scale=N)` (the documented way to rasterise an EPS at higher resolution) renders `width*N × height*N` pixels through Ghostscript, but the only decompression-bomb check on the way is the one `Image.open()` ran on the *unscaled*, file-declared `width × height`. The scaled product is never passed to `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` before `gs` is started. This 111-byte EPS declares 9000×9000 = 81,000,000 pixels, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (89,478,485), so `Image.open()` accepts it without even a warning: ``` %!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0 %%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000 %%EndComments 0 0 moveto 9000 9000 lineto stroke showpage ``` `im.load(scale=2)` on it then executes ``` gs -q -g18000x18000 -r144.000000x144.000000 -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -sDEVICE=pnmraw -sOutputFile=/tmp/tmpXXXX -c 0 0 translate -f attack.eps -c showpage ``` i.e. asks Ghostscript for an 18000×18000 = 324,000,000-pixel raster (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`), whose `pnmraw` output is a 972,000,019-byte file in the temp directory. An EPS that declares 18000×18000 directly is rejected by `Image.open()` with `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is ever run; via `scale=2` the same raster is rendered first and the `DecompressionBombError` only appears afterwards, when Pillow opens the file Ghostscript produced. (Between 1× and 2× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, `Image.open()` only emits `DecompressionBombWarning`, so with the default warning filter an EPS declaring e.g. 13377×13377 is already rendered at `scale=1` — a 537 MB PNM. Against that baseline, `scale=2` is 4× an already-permitted render.) The arithmetic is in `Ghostscript()`: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:91-97 # Hack to support hi-res rendering scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:139-142 command = [ gs_binary, "-q", # quiet mode f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}", # set output geometry (pixels) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:165-168 subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo) with Image.open(outfile) as out_im: out_im.load() return out_im.im.copy() ``` and its caller does nothing between taking `scale` from the application and invoking it: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:411-417 def load(self, scale: int = 1, transparency: bool = False) -> …: # Load EPS via Ghostscript if self.tile: assert self.fp is not None self.im = Ghostscript(self.tile, self.size, self.fp, scale, transparency) ``` `size` here is `self._size`, computed in `_open()` from the file's `%%BoundingBox` (or `%ImageData`) and checked once by `Image.open()` at `src/PIL/Image.py:3700`. For the benign path (`scale=1`) that check covers exactly what Ghostscript is asked to render. For `scale=N` the rendered pixel count is N² times what was checked, so a file can sit just under the limit at open time and have Ghostscript render 4× (scale 2), 9× (scale 3), 16× (scale 4) the configured budget. The first point at which Pillow looks at the real size again is `Image.open(outfile)` at line 166 — after `subprocess.check_call` has returned, i.e. after Ghostscript has spent the CPU and written `width*height*3` bytes to `tempfile.mkstemp()`'s directory. `WmfStubImageFile.load(dpi)` has the same shape (file-derived extent × caller-supplied factor → new raster) and, since af70b075a, calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)` on the recomputed size before rendering (`src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:127-131`). The EPS path lacks the equivalent line. The gap dates from ce2955ec7128 ("Throw an exception when an opened image is larger than an arbitrary limit", 2014-05-14, first released in 2.5.0), which added the check to `Image.open()` without covering the `scale` path. ## Impact Affected are applications that open untrusted EPS/PS with Ghostscript installed and call `load(scale=N)` with a fixed N > 1, as the handbook suggests for non-blurry output. Handing untrusted EPS to Ghostscript at all already lets the same attacker tie up a worker with an equally tiny file (e.g. a PostScript `{} loop`; Pillow runs `gs` with no timeout), so this bug adds a constant factor rather than a new denial-of-service capability. Within that setting, a ~110-byte upload makes each request run Ghostscript over N² × `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` pixels (N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` if the application does not turn `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error) and write a `W·H·3`-byte PNM into the temp directory — 972 MB for the example above at scale 2, 2.2 GB at scale 3, 8.6 GB for a 178-Mpixel declaration at scale 4 — before any limit is applied. The operator's `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` setting is exceeded by a factor of N²; N is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file, so the work stays bounded at N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. The consequence is N² more Ghostscript CPU and temp-disk use per request than the configured limit intends; Pillow's own in-process pixel allocation remains bounded because `Image.open(outfile)` re-checks the PNM's size, and there is no memory corruption. This is a sibling of the WMF `load(dpi)` issue fixed in af70b075a ("Add decompression bomb check when loading at a different DPI"); the EPS `scale` path was not covered by that change. Unlike the WMF case, where the file-controlled `_inch` makes the ratio unbounded, the EPS multiplier is fixed by the application. ## Reproducing Run `repro` against the installed Pillow. Ghostscript does not need to be installed: the script sets `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs"` so that `has_ghostscript()` skips its `gs --version` probe, and replaces `subprocess.check_call` with a function that records the command line Pillow builds and then raises `OSError`, so nothing is actually rendered. It writes a 76-byte EPS declaring `%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000` (the example above without the drawing line; 81 Mpixel, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` of 89,478,485) and turns `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error, so any bomb check — warning or hard error — counts. It then calls `Image.open()` and `im.load(scale=2)`. `Image.open()` accepts the file and `load(scale=2)` reaches the intercepted Ghostscript call with `-g18000x18000` (324,000,000 pixels, 3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, a 972 MB `pnmraw` output with real Ghostscript). The script prints the geometry it captured. It prints `BUG` when Ghostscript was invoked with a `-g` geometry above `2*MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178,956,970) and no decompression-bomb check fired before that call; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, `load(scale=2)` raises `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is called and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch checks the scaled size in `Ghostscript()` right after the scaled `width`/`height` are computed (`src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:93-94`) and before the `gs` command is built, mirroring `WmfStubImageFile.load`: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` `load(scale=N)` now raises `DecompressionBombError` / emits `DecompressionBombWarning` under the same `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` thresholds `Image.open()` applies, before Ghostscript runs instead of after. Placing the check in `Ghostscript()` rather than in `EpsImageFile.load()` is the single point where the rendered extent is decided, so it also covers direct callers of the module-level function. With the patch applied to a clean checkout the reproducer prints `OK` and `Tests/test_file_eps.py` passes. One cosmetic side effect: at `scale=1` the check re-emits the `DecompressionBombWarning` that `Image.open()` already issued for sizes between 1× and 2× the limit; guarding the call with `if scale > 1:` would avoid the duplicate. The patch also adds `test_load_scale_decompression_bomb` to `Tests/test_file_eps.py`, in the style of the WMF test: it sets `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` to `im.width * im.height` and expects `im.load(scale=2)` to raise `DecompressionBombError`. Like the rest of that file it is skipped without Ghostscript, because `has_ghostscript()` is consulted at the top of `Ghostscript()`; moving the check above that call would let the test run without it. ## The patch Add decompression bomb check on the scaled size in EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() before Ghostscript is invoked Applies to `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_eps.py b/Tests/test_file_eps.py index 70eced62a..de331d97f 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_eps.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_eps.py @@ -98,6 +98,14 @@ def test_sanity(filename: str, size: tuple[int, int], scale: int) -> None: assert image.format == "EPS" +@pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") +def test_load_scale_decompression_bomb(monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None: + with Image.open(FILE1) as im: + monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", im.width * im.height) + with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError): + im.load(scale=2) + + @pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") def test_load() -> None: with Image.open(FILE1) as im: diff --git a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py index 5eaefe339..ccc6f1d85 100644 --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,845 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript(): load(scale=N) hands gs a -g geometry of # (W*N)x(H*N) with no _decompression_bomb_check on the scaled size; only the # unscaled WxH was checked by Image.open(). gs is not installed here, so we # set gs_binary and intercept subprocess.check_call to read the argv Pillow builds. import os, subprocess, tempfile, warnings from PIL import Image, EpsImagePlugin EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs" # skip the `gs --version` probe path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "a.eps") with open(path, "w") as f: # 9000x9000 = 81 Mpx < MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (89.5 Mpx) f.write("%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0\n%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000\n%%EndComments\nshowpage\n") calls = [] def fake_check_call(cmd, **kw): calls.append(cmd) raise OSError("gs intercepted") # stop here; we only need the argv subprocess.check_call = fake_check_call hard = 2 * Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS bomb_before_gs = False with warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("error", Image.DecompressionBombWarning) try: with Image.open(path) as im: print("Image.open accepted", os.path.getsize(path), "byte EPS, size", im.size) im.load(scale=2) except (Image.DecompressionBombError, Image.DecompressionBombWarning) as e: bomb_before_gs = not calls print("bomb check fired", "before" if bomb_before_gs else "after", "gs:", e) except OSError as e: print("load() reached gs:", e) over = False for c in calls: g = next(a for a in c if a.startswith("-g"))[2:] w, h = map(int, g.split("x")) over |= w * h > hard print(f"gs argv geometry -g{g} = {w*h} px ({w*h/Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS:.1f}x MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, " f"hard limit {hard}); pnmraw output would be {w*h*3} bytes") print("BUG" if calls and over and not bomb_before_gs else "OK") ```

vulnerabilities.summary: pip's fallback tar extraction doesn't check symbolic links point to extraction directory
vulnerabilities.details: When extracting a tar archive pip may not check symbolic links point into the extraction directory if the tarfile module doesn't implement PEP 706. Note that upgrading pip to a "fixed" version for this vulnerability doesn't fix all known vulnerabilities that are remediated by using a Python version that implements PEP 706. Note that this is a vulnerability in pip's fallback implementation of tar extraction for Python versions that don't implement PEP 706 and therefore are not secure to all vulnerabilities in the Python 'tarfile' module. If you're using a Python version that implements PEP 706 then pip doesn't use the "vulnerable" fallback code. Mitigations include upgrading to a version of pip that includes the fix, upgrading to a Python version that implements PEP 706 (Python >=3.9.17, >=3.10.12, >=3.11.4, or >=3.12), applying the linked patch, or inspecting source distributions (sdists) before installation as is already a best-practice.

vulnerabilities.summary: pip has an interpretation conflict due to handling both concatenated tar and ZIP files as ZIP files
vulnerabilities.details: pip handles concatenated tar and ZIP files as ZIP files regardless of filename or whether a file is both a tar and ZIP file. This behavior could result in confusing installation behavior, such as installing "incorrect" files according to the filename of the archive. New behavior only proceeds with installation if the file identifies uniquely as a ZIP or tar archive, not as both.

vulnerabilities.summary: pip Path Traversal vulnerability
vulnerabilities.details: When pip is installing and extracting a maliciously crafted wheel archive, files may be extracted outside the installation directory. The path traversal is limited to prefixes of the installation directory, thus isn't able to inject or overwrite executable files in typical situations.

vulnerabilities.summary: pip Vulnerable to Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
vulnerabilities.details: pip prior to version 26.1 would run self-update check functionality after installing wheel files which required importing well-known Python modules names. These module imports were intentionally deferred to increase startup time of the pip CLI. The patch changes self-update functionality to run before wheels are installed to prevent newly-installed modules from being imported shortly after the installation of a wheel package. Users should still review package contents prior to installation.

vulnerabilities.summary: pip would incorrectly handle doubly-encoded package URLs from indexes
vulnerabilities.details:
pip would incorrectly handle doubly-encoded package URLs from indexes allowing for files to be installed to arbitrary locations on disk even when installing wheels.

This vulnerability requires downloading or installing a package from a malicious package index to succeed, malicious packages alone are not able to exploit this vulnerability. Note that this vulnerability only materially impacts users running `pip download` with the `--only-binary` option as installing source distributions from an untrusted index is already an unsafe operation that executes code during install time.

vulnerabilities.summary: pip: Path traversal in console_scripts/gui_scripts entry point names allows installing scripts outside of target directory
vulnerabilities.details: pip would treat console_scripts and gui_scripts as paths instead of file names without sanitizing the resolved absolute path to the installation directory, leading to entry points being installed outside the installation directory.

vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

An attacker who uses this vulnerability can craft a PDF which leads to long runtimes and large memory consumption. This requires accessing the outlines of a document with either lots of entries or nested outlines with long re-used nesting paths.

### Patches

This has been fixed in [pypdf==6.16.1](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/releases/tag/6.16.1).

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, consider applying the changes from PR [#3966](https://github.com/py-pdf/pypdf/pull/3966).

vulnerabilities.summary: urllib3: HTTPS proxy TLS configuration may be ignored or overridden
vulnerabilities.details:
## Impact

urllib3 supports configuring TLS independently for an HTTPS proxy and the target server.

`proxy_ssl_context`, `proxy_assert_hostname`, and `proxy_assert_fingerprint` configure the TLS connection to the proxy. `ssl_context` and the other target-specific TLS parameters configure the connection to the target server.

In urllib3 versions 1.26.0 through 2.7.0, these configurations were not consistently separated. Depending on the proxy mode, urllib3 could:

1. Ignore `proxy_ssl_context` and use the target server's SSL context for the TLS connection to an HTTPS forwarding proxy.
2. Override the HTTPS proxy's certificate-verification policy with the target server's certificate-verification policy.
3. Apply target-specific SNI, hostname assertions, certificate fingerprint assertions, or TLS client credentials to the TLS connection to an HTTPS forwarding proxy.

In particular, configuring `cert_reqs="CERT_NONE"` for a target server could overwrite the `verify_mode` of the SSL context configured for the HTTPS proxy. This modification occurred in place and persisted on the context object, potentially disabling proxy certificate verification for later connections that reused the same context.

An attacker able to intercept the connection to an HTTPS proxy may be able to impersonate the proxy when the effective proxy TLS configuration disables certificate verification or otherwise accepts the attacker's certificate. This may occur, for example, when the target server's trust or identity policy is incorrectly applied to the proxy connection.

When HTTPS forwarding is enabled, an impersonated proxy can observe or modify forwarded requests and responses, potentially exposing credentials, authentication tokens, request bodies, response data, and other sensitive information.

A TLS client certificate intended for the target server may also be presented to the proxy or to an attacker impersonating it. This can disclose the client's identity and provide proof of possession of the corresponding private key. The private key itself is not transmitted during the TLS handshake.

In CONNECT tunneling mode, impersonating the HTTPS proxy does not by itself defeat the separate end-to-end TLS connection between the client and the target server.

## Affected Usages

Code using urllib3 versions 1.26.0 through 2.7.0 may be affected in any of the following cases.

### 1. The target SSL context is used for an HTTPS forwarding proxy

HTTPS requests are forwarded through an HTTPS proxy with `use_forwarding_for_https=True`, and `proxy_ssl_context` is configured for the proxy.

urllib3 may ignore `proxy_ssl_context` and use the target server's `ssl_context` for the proxy TLS handshake. The proxy may therefore be verified using the target server's trust and certificate policy instead of the policy explicitly configured for the proxy.

### 2. The target verification policy overrides the proxy policy

An HTTPS proxy is configured with `proxy_ssl_context`, while the target server uses a different certificate-verification policy.

urllib3 may apply the target server's `cert_reqs` value to the proxy SSL context. For example, setting `cert_reqs="CERT_NONE"` for the target server may also disable certificate verification for the HTTPS proxy, even when `proxy_ssl_context` was configured to require verification.

This issue can affect the TLS connection to an HTTPS proxy in both forwarding and CONNECT tunneling configurations.

### 3. A mutated proxy SSL context is reused

The same SSL context is reused as `proxy_ssl_context` across multiple connections, and certificate verification is disabled for one target server.

urllib3 may modify the proxy SSL context's `verify_mode` in place. Later connections that reuse the same context may therefore connect to the HTTPS proxy without certificate verification.

### 4. Target-specific TLS identity or credentials are applied to the proxy

HTTPS requests are forwarded through an HTTPS proxy with `use_forwarding_for_https=True`, and target-specific SNI, hostname assertions, certificate fingerprint assertions, or TLS client credentials are configured.

urllib3 may apply these target-specific settings to the proxy TLS handshake. This may cause urllib3 to:

- send SNI intended for the target server to the proxy;
- verify the proxy using a hostname or certificate fingerprint intended for the target server; or
- present a TLS client certificate intended for the target server to the proxy.

Code connecting through a plain HTTP proxy does not establish a TLS connection to the proxy and is not affected by this issue.

## Remediation

Upgrade to urllib3 2.8.0 or later.

urllib3 2.8.0 independently applies the explicitly configured `proxy_ssl_context` and proxy-specific certificate assertions to the HTTPS proxy connection. Target-specific SNI, certificate assertions, and TLS client certificate parameters are no longer applied to the HTTPS proxy handshake.

For backward compatibility, when an HTTPS proxy is used with `use_forwarding_for_https=True` and `proxy_ssl_context` is not provided, urllib3 2.8.0 continues to use `ssl_context` for the TLS connection to the proxy. This configuration emits a `FutureWarning`. In urllib3 3.0, passing `ssl_context` with `use_forwarding_for_https=True` for an HTTPS proxy will raise an error. Applications should use `proxy_ssl_context` to configure TLS for an HTTPS forwarding proxy.

The fixes were implemented in commits b6447295fff7b38fdffc67e0df9712d60cef3cc3 and 07408cec79d1856d81bb42c74a904a24fdb9e465.

vulnerabilities.summary: urllib3: Chunked Deflate streaming can enter an infinite loop
vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

urllib3's streaming API is designed for the efficient handling of large HTTP responses by reading content in chunks instead of loading the entire response body into memory at once.

urllib3 can decompress response bodies according to the HTTP `Content-Encoding` header. When streaming a compressed, chunked response, urllib3 first consumes data already buffered by the decoder before reading the next HTTP chunk.

However, urllib3 versions from 2.6.2 through 2.7.0 could enter an infinite loop when a chunked response contained bytes after the end of the Deflate stream. If the decompressed body exceeded the requested streaming chunk size, Python's zlib implementation could retain the trailing bytes as unconsumed input after reaching the end of the compressed stream. urllib3 would repeatedly attempt to decode those same bytes without making progress or reading more data from the network.

A malicious server could exploit this behavior to cause excessive CPU usage and prevent the affected request from completing on the client. Network read timeouts would not interrupt the loop because no further socket operation was required.

### Affected usages

Applications and libraries using urllib3 versions 2.6.2 through 2.7.0 may be affected when all of the following conditions are met:

1. Compressed responses from an untrusted source are streamed using `HTTPResponse.stream(amt=N)` or `HTTPResponse.read_chunked(amt=N)` with a positive, finite chunk size.
2. Content decoding is enabled.
3. The response uses both `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and `Content-Encoding: deflate`.
4. The decoded body exceeds the requested chunk size and the encoded body contains bytes after the end of the Deflate stream.

`HTTPResponse.stream()` uses a finite chunk size by default and is therefore affected when the other conditions are met.

### Remediation

Upgrade to urllib3 2.8.0, in which the Deflate decoder stops accepting input after reaching the end of the compressed stream and no longer reports trailing bytes as data that can produce more decoded output.

If upgrading is not immediately possible, disable automatic content decoding for responses from untrusted sources by setting `decode_content=False`, or reject streamed responses using the Deflate content encoding. Applications that disable automatic decoding must handle the compressed response safely at another layer.

vulnerabilities.summary: urllib3: HTTPResponse.stream()/read_chunked() buffers an unbounded chunk-size line into memory
vulnerabilities.details:
## Impact

urllib3's [streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/2.7.0/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o) is designed for efficiently handling large HTTP responses by reading the content in chunks, rather than loading the entire response body into memory at once. When decoding a [chunked-transfer-encoded response](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9112.html#chunked.encoding), this API reads each chunk's size field by buffering until it sees `\n` or EOF.

A malicious HTTP server can return `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and then send a very long run of bytes without any newline, causing the streaming client to buffer that entire run before urllib3 can reject the chunk size as invalid and allocate more memory than intended.

To fix the issue, we'll reject chunk-size fields larger than 65536 bytes, as already done in the non-streaming case, which is currently handled by the Python standard library. Note that this only applies to reading the chunk-size field, not the chunk data, which is already handled correctly. Thus, there shouldn't be any impact for non-malicious servers.

## Affected usages

Applications and libraries using urllib3 versions earlier than 2.8.0 may be affected when streaming a chunked response from untrusted sources. Specifically, this affects the [read_chunked()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read_chunked) and [stream()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.stream) methods of the HTTPResponse object.

This also affects requests streaming API, which uses urllib3 under the hood.

## Remediation

Upgrade to urllib3 version 2.8.0 or later, where chunk-size fields larger than 65536 will be rejected. If upgrading is not immediately possible, consider reading the response at once using the [read()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read) method.

2. Override the HTTPS proxy's certificate-verification policy with the target server's certificate-verification policy.
3. Apply target-specific SNI, hostname assertions, certificate fingerprint assertions, or TLS client credentials to the TLS connection to an HTTPS forwarding proxy.

In particular, configuring `cert_reqs="CERT_NONE"` for a target server could overwrite the `verify_mode` of the SSL context configured for the HTTPS proxy. This modification occurred in place and persisted on the context object, potentially disabling proxy certificate verification for later connections that reused the same context.

An attacker able to intercept the connection to an HTTPS proxy may be able to impersonate the proxy when the effective proxy TLS configuration disables certificate verification or otherwise accepts the attacker's certificate. This may occur, for example, when the target server's trust or identity policy is incorrectly applied to the proxy connection.

When HTTPS forwarding is enabled, an impersonated proxy can observe or modify forwarded requests and responses, potentially exposing credentials, authentication tokens, request bodies, response data, and other sensitive information.

A TLS client certificate intended for the target server may also be presented to the proxy or to an attacker impersonating it. This can disclose the client's identity and provide proof of possession of the corresponding private key. The private key itself is not transmitted during the TLS handshake.

In CONNECT tunneling mode, impersonating the HTTPS proxy does not by itself defeat the separate end-to-end TLS connection between the client and the target server.

## Affected Usages

Code using urllib3 versions 1.26.0 through 2.7.0 may be affected in any of the following cases.

### 1. The target SSL context is used for an HTTPS forwarding proxy

HTTPS requests are forwarded through an HTTPS proxy with `use_forwarding_for_https=True`, and `proxy_ssl_context` is configured for the proxy.

urllib3 may ignore `proxy_ssl_context` and use the target server's `ssl_context` for the proxy TLS handshake. The proxy may therefore be verified using the target server's trust and certificate policy instead of the policy explicitly configured for the proxy.

### 2. The target verification policy overrides the proxy policy

An HTTPS proxy is configured with `proxy_ssl_context`, while the target server uses a different certificate-verification policy.

urllib3 may apply the target server's `cert_reqs` value to the proxy SSL context. For example, setting `cert_reqs="CERT_NONE"` for the target server may also disable certificate verification for the HTTPS proxy, even when `proxy_ssl_context` was configured to require verification.

This issue can affect the TLS connection to an HTTPS proxy in both forwarding and CONNECT tunneling configurations.

### 3. A mutated proxy SSL context is reused

The same SSL context is reused as `proxy_ssl_context` across multiple connections, and certificate verification is disabled for one target server.

urllib3 may modify the proxy SSL context's `verify_mode` in place. Later connections that reuse the same context may therefore connect to the HTTPS proxy without certificate verification.

### 4. Target-specific TLS identity or credentials are applied to the proxy

HTTPS requests are forwarded through an HTTPS proxy with `use_forwarding_for_https=True`, and target-specific SNI, hostname assertions, certificate fingerprint assertions, or TLS client credentials are configured.

urllib3 may apply these target-specific settings to the proxy TLS handshake. This may cause urllib3 to:

- send SNI intended for the target server to the proxy;
- verify the proxy using a hostname or certificate fingerprint intended for the target server; or
- present a TLS client certificate intended for the target server to the proxy.

Code connecting through a plain HTTP proxy does not establish a TLS connection to the proxy and is not affected by this issue.

## Remediation

Upgrade to urllib3 2.8.0 or later.

urllib3 2.8.0 independently applies the explicitly configured `proxy_ssl_context` and proxy-specific certificate assertions to the HTTPS proxy connection. Target-specific SNI, certificate assertions, and TLS client certificate parameters are no longer applied to the HTTPS proxy handshake.

For backward compatibility, when an HTTPS proxy is used with `use_forwarding_for_https=True` and `proxy_ssl_context` is not provided, urllib3 2.8.0 continues to use `ssl_context` for the TLS connection to the proxy. This configuration emits a `FutureWarning`. In urllib3 3.0, passing `ssl_context` with `use_forwarding_for_https=True` for an HTTPS proxy will raise an error. Applications should use `proxy_ssl_context` to configure TLS for an HTTPS forwarding proxy.

The fixes were implemented in commits b6447295fff7b38fdffc67e0df9712d60cef3cc3 and 07408cec79d1856d81bb42c74a904a24fdb9e465.

vulnerabilities.summary: urllib3: Chunked Deflate streaming can enter an infinite loop
vulnerabilities.details:
### Impact

urllib3's streaming API is designed for the efficient handling of large HTTP responses by reading content in chunks instead of loading the entire response body into memory at once.

urllib3 can decompress response bodies according to the HTTP `Content-Encoding` header. When streaming a compressed, chunked response, urllib3 first consumes data already buffered by the decoder before reading the next HTTP chunk.

However, urllib3 versions from 2.6.2 through 2.7.0 could enter an infinite loop when a chunked response contained bytes after the end of the Deflate stream. If the decompressed body exceeded the requested streaming chunk size, Python's zlib implementation could retain the trailing bytes as unconsumed input after reaching the end of the compressed stream. urllib3 would repeatedly attempt to decode those same bytes without making progress or reading more data from the network.

A malicious server could exploit this behavior to cause excessive CPU usage and prevent the affected request from completing on the client. Network read timeouts would not interrupt the loop because no further socket operation was required.

### Affected usages

Applications and libraries using urllib3 versions 2.6.2 through 2.7.0 may be affected when all of the following conditions are met:

1. Compressed responses from an untrusted source are streamed using `HTTPResponse.stream(amt=N)` or `HTTPResponse.read_chunked(amt=N)` with a positive, finite chunk size.
2. Content decoding is enabled.
3. The response uses both `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and `Content-Encoding: deflate`.
4. The decoded body exceeds the requested chunk size and the encoded body contains bytes after the end of the Deflate stream.

`HTTPResponse.stream()` uses a finite chunk size by default and is therefore affected when the other conditions are met.

### Remediation

Upgrade to urllib3 2.8.0, in which the Deflate decoder stops accepting input after reaching the end of the compressed stream and no longer reports trailing bytes as data that can produce more decoded output.

If upgrading is not immediately possible, disable automatic content decoding for responses from untrusted sources by setting `decode_content=False`, or reject streamed responses using the Deflate content encoding. Applications that disable automatic decoding must handle the compressed response safely at another layer.

vulnerabilities.summary: urllib3: HTTPResponse.stream()/read_chunked() buffers an unbounded chunk-size line into memory
vulnerabilities.details:
## Impact

urllib3's [streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/2.7.0/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o) is designed for efficiently handling large HTTP responses by reading the content in chunks, rather than loading the entire response body into memory at once. When decoding a [chunked-transfer-encoded response](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9112.html#chunked.encoding), this API reads each chunk's size field by buffering until it sees `\n` or EOF.

A malicious HTTP server can return `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and then send a very long run of bytes without any newline, causing the streaming client to buffer that entire run before urllib3 can reject the chunk size as invalid and allocate more memory than intended.

To fix the issue, we'll reject chunk-size fields larger than 65536 bytes, as already done in the non-streaming case, which is currently handled by the Python standard library. Note that this only applies to reading the chunk-size field, not the chunk data, which is already handled correctly. Thus, there shouldn't be any impact for non-malicious servers.

## Affected usages

Applications and libraries using urllib3 versions earlier than 2.8.0 may be affected when streaming a chunked response from untrusted sources. Specifically, this affects the [read_chunked()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read_chunked) and [stream()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.stream) methods of the HTTPResponse object.

This also affects requests streaming API, which uses urllib3 under the hood.

## Remediation

Upgrade to urllib3 version 2.8.0 or later, where chunk-size fields larger than 65536 will be rejected. If upgrading is not immediately possible, consider reading the response at once using the [read()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read) method.
